h1: BMR - Mifflin St Jeor equation Calculator
summary: The BMR - Mifflin St Jeor equation calculator is a free, no-sign-up health tool. Fill in the 8 fields it asks for and it works out BMR (Basal metabolic rate) (Results) straight away, with the formula shown underneath. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the BMR - Mifflin St Jeor equation calculator work?
sections.html:
The BMR - Mifflin St Jeor equation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports BMR (Basal metabolic rate) (Results) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the BMR formula, the sex and the show additional information); then you type in the BMR (Basal metabolic rate) (Results), the BMR (Basal metabolic rate) (Results), the BMR (Basal metabolic rate) (Results) and the BMR (Basal metabolic rate) (Results).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the BMR - Mifflin St Jeor equation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

BMR (Basal metabolic rate)=-5 × age + 625 × height + 10 × weight + 5
Lean body mass=(5 ÷ 108) × BMR (Basal metabolic rate) − 925 ÷ 54
BMR (Basal metabolic rate)=-5677 ÷ 1000 × age + (4799 ÷ 10) × height + (13397 ÷ 1000) × weight + 44181 ÷ 500
Weight=(4330 ÷ 9247) × age + (1000 ÷ 9247) × BMR (Basal metabolic rate) − 309800 ÷ 9247 × height − 447593 ÷ 9247
Weight=(33775 ÷ 68758) × age + (2500 ÷ 34379) × BMR (Basal metabolic rate) − 1250825 ÷ 34379 × height − 332365 ÷ 68758
Weight=(23378 ÷ 47817) × age + (5000 ÷ 47817) × BMR (Basal metabolic rate) − 924800 ÷ 47817 × height − 6550955 ÷ 95634

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The BMR - Mifflin St Jeor equation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the BMR (Basal metabolic rate) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the BMR - Mifflin St Jeor equation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns BMR (Basal metabolic rate) (Results), derived from the BMR (Basal metabolic rate). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the BMR - Mifflin St Jeor equation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the BMR (Basal metabolic rate), which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter height in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Height opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the BMR - Mifflin St Jeor equation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
